transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, it’s... it’s a bit hard to explain, I suppose, because at my age—I’m 70 now, you know, and I haven't worked in quite a long time—most people think you just sit in a comfortable chair and watch the world go by. But my daughter actually suggested I come talk to someone because I just... I never seem to stop. I feel like I’m always up and moving around the house, from the minute I wake up until the evening. 

Like, just the other day, which was supposed to be a completely quiet Tuesday, absolutely nothing on the calendar, I found myself just bouncing from one thing to the next without a second's rest. I started looking at the contact list for my garden club—I've been helping them organize the spring plant sale, which is a whole ordeal on its own with the weather we've been having, let me tell you—but before I even finished checking the first few names, I was suddenly over by the sofa digging through my knitting bag. I had remembered this lovely cable-knit pattern I wanted to try for a scarf. And then, well, I didn't even get the yarn pulled out of the bag before I was up again, standing at the kitchen table shuffling through all these travel papers and brochures for a trip we're trying to plan. 

It’s just... I do this all day long. I just keep moving and shifting from thing to thing before I’ve really finished any one of them. It's like I have a motor running that won't let me just sit and enjoy my retirement.
Has this tendency to jump from task to task always been a part of your personality since you were younger, or is this something that has started more recently?

Oh, my, no, it’s certainly not new. Not at all. If I really sit down and think about it—which, as I just told you, is quite the chore for me to begin with!—it’s been this way for as long as I can remember. I mean, all the way back to when I was just a little girl. 

You know, back in grade school, I remember my mother coming home from parent-teacher conferences. I think it was third grade... or maybe fourth? It might have been Mrs. Higgins' class, she was lovely but very strict about posture. Anyway, the teachers would always tell my mother the exact same thing, year after year. They’d say I was a bright girl, which was nice of them, but that I was just completely scattered. I was always, always losing my school papers. My desk was just a disaster of crumpled up assignments and broken pencils. 

And I simply could not keep quiet. I was constantly talking out of turn, just blurting things out when I was supposed to be listening to the lesson or waiting to be called on. And the wiggling! Oh, my mother used to just sigh and shake her head about it. The teachers said I was always wiggling around in my seat, just squirming and shifting constantly, and I’d be up out of my chair before I had even finished my work. It was like sitting still was a physical impossibility for me, even back then. I just had to be doing something else, moving on to the next thing. 

So, yes, it’s always been a part of who I am. It’s funny, isn't it, how you carry these things with you your whole life? You’d think by the time you reach seventy, you would have finally settled down and learned to just sit by the fire, but here I am, still acting exactly like that same squirmy little girl who couldn't just finish one spelling worksheet before getting up to see what everyone else was doing.
